title: Why Almost Nobody Lives in Northern Maine

chapters.title: Half a State With No Towns

paragraphs.text: Maine is the corner of the United States that pushes up into Canada. It is nearly as big as the other five New England states put together. It is also the only state that borders just one other state. About one point four million people live there, and most of them live in the south, near the coast. The two southern counties around Portland hold almost four in ten Mainers on about a twentieth of the land. Go north and it changes. At night, from orbit, the north of Maine is almost completely dark.

stat.label: Maine's total area; the other five New England states together: 36,608
stat.source: US Census Bureau state areas (our sum)

stat.label: Mainers living in Cumberland and York counties, on about 6 % of the land (2020)
stat.source: US Census Bureau, 2020 census and Gazetteer (our sum)

paragraphs.text: Almost half of Maine has no town government at all. No mayor, no town council, no town. The Census calls it unorganized territory: more than fourteen thousand square miles of land, bigger than the whole state of Maryland. At the last census about eight thousand three hundred people lived in all of it. That is fewer than one person per square mile. The biggest single piece, in the northwest, covers more than two and a half thousand square miles, more than the whole state of Delaware. Twelve people live there.

stat.label: Share of Maine's land with no town government: 14,264 square miles
stat.source: US Census Bureau, 2020 census and Gazetteer (our sum)

stat.label: People living in all of Maine's unorganized territory, 2020 census (our sum)
stat.source: US Census Bureau, 2020 census and Gazetteer (our sum)

paragraphs.text: It is not that the land is worthless. It is the most forested state in the country. Britain and America nearly went to war over this forest. A town up here lost nearly nine of every ten people. And one man bought its highest mountain and gave it away, on one condition. So why does almost nobody live in northern Maine? There are five reasons. The first is that the land was sold before anyone got there.

shots.on_screen_text: Forest and lakes near Moosehead in October
The St. John River, on the border with Canada

paragraphs.text: Reason one. The land was sold before anyone got there. After the American Revolution, Maine was not a state. It belonged to Massachusetts, and Massachusetts was broke. It owed a war debt it could not pay. What it did have was millions of acres of forest in the north. So it sold them. In 1786 it even ran a lottery: fifty townships, cut into two thousand seven hundred and sixty lots. A Philadelphia banker named William Bingham ended up with two tracts of about a million acres each.

shots.on_screen_text: Forest north of the Penobscot in October

stat.label: Fifty townships of Maine forest, sold by lottery, 1786

shots.on_screen_text: Forest in central Maine in October
The upper Kennebec, part of Bingham's purchase

stat.label: William Bingham's two Maine tracts, about a million acres each

paragraphs.text: Surveyors cut the woods into a grid of squares, and many of those squares never got names. Look at a map of northern Maine today and you still see them: T3 R13 WELS. Township three, range thirteen, west of the east line of the state. A grid of numbers where, in other states, there would be towns. The state itself runs these places. There is no one else to do it.

shots.on_screen_text: Numbered townships west of Chesuncook Lake

shots.photo: File:Access to the areas of study was limited by private logging roads. A team is shown here staging for a hike into a area where Canada Lynx are known to be "denning". (4700060450).jpg

paragraphs.text: When Maine became a state in 1820, it split the remaining public land with Massachusetts, and both kept selling. In 1853 Maine bought out what Massachusetts still held, about one point two million acres, and kept on selling too. The buyers were not families looking for farms. They were lumbermen, and later paper companies. For most of the twentieth century, a dozen or so companies and families owned around twelve million acres of northern Maine. One of them, Great Northern Paper, held more than two million acres by the 1940s.

stat.label: Maine becomes a state and splits the public land with Massachusetts
Land Maine bought back from Massachusetts in 1853

shots.on_screen_text: Forest north of Millinocket in October
Ripogenus Dam, built by Great Northern Paper

stat.label: Northern Maine owned by about a dozen companies and families, most of the 1900s
stat.source: Natural Resources Council of Maine; press reports

shots.on_screen_text: Company forest, northern Maine in October
The West Branch of the Penobscot below Katahdin

paragraphs.text: Those owners have changed, but the pattern has not. From the 1990s the paper companies began selling their land, and much of it went to investment funds, pension funds and timber investment groups. Some old owners stayed. One family company, Seven Islands, still manages about a million acres for dozens of members of the Pingree family. And in 2016 a single family trust bought nearly three hundred thousand acres of the north woods in one deal. Up here, forest changes hands in blocks the size of whole counties elsewhere.

shots.on_screen_text: Chesuncook Lake, in the North Woods
Working forest, northern Maine in winter
Working forest near the Quebec border in October

stat.label: Forest managed by Seven Islands Land Company for the Pingree family

shots.on_screen_text: Forest in the Allagash country in winter

stat.label: North Woods land bought by one family trust in 2016

shots.on_screen_text: Forest west of the Aroostook valley in October

paragraphs.text: Companies do not build towns where they do not need people to live. They build roads. In 1971 Great Northern finished the Golden Road, almost a hundred miles of private gravel from its mill at Millinocket west to the Quebec border, built for log trucks. That same year the landowners set up a group called North Maine Woods to run the gates. There are nineteen of them. Today about three and a half million acres are managed that way. Every road inside is private. To drive in, you stop at a checkpoint and pay a fee, as you would at a park. Except this park is somebody's tree farm.

shots.on_screen_text: A logging road in the North Woods

stat.label: Checkpoints into the North Maine Woods, run by the landowners since 1971
Private forest behind the North Maine Woods gates

shots.on_screen_text: A logging road junction in October
A gravel road in the North Woods in winter
Cutting blocks on private forest in winter

paragraphs.text: Before any of it was sold, this was Wabanaki land: the Penobscot, the Passamaquoddy, the Maliseet and the Mi'kmaq. In the 1970s two of those nations went to court and claimed about twelve million acres, nearly two thirds of the state. In 1980 the federal government settled for eighty-one and a half million dollars, mostly so the tribes could buy back about three hundred thousand acres. So half of Maine was never really a place where people settled. It was a place where wood was grown. But first, somebody had to decide which country it was in.

shots.on_screen_text: Indian Island, home of the Penobscot Nation
Sipayik, Passamaquoddy land on Passamaquoddy Bay

stat.label: Land claimed by the Passamaquoddy and Penobscot: nearly two thirds of Maine
Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, 1980: money to buy back about 300,000 acres

shots.on_screen_text: Forest along the East Branch of the Penobscot
Forest near the Quebec border in October

paragraphs.text: Reason two. Nobody knew where the border was. The treaty that ended the Revolution in 1783 drew the line between the United States and British Canada with words, not surveys: north from the source of the St. Croix River to the highlands that divide the rivers running to the St. Lawrence from those running to the Atlantic. Historians later called it so badly worded that it could not be turned into a real line on the ground.

shots.on_screen_text: The highlands on the Quebec border

document.text: ...the Treaty of 1783 was so badly worded that it could not be translated into a practical topographical boundary.
document.source: Keenleyside and Brown, Canada and the United States

shots.photo: File:Map of the disputed territory reduced from the original of Messrs Featherstonhaugh & Mudge - British commissioners - btv1b8495488t.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The disputed territory, a British commissioners' map

paragraphs.text: Americans read it one way, the British another. The Americans said the line ran almost to the St. Lawrence. The British said it stopped near a hill in Aroostook called Mars Hill. Between the two readings lay about twelve thousand square miles of forest that both countries claimed. In 1831 they asked the King of the Netherlands to settle it. He split the land, roughly two thirds to the Americans and one third to the British. The United States turned his answer down.

stat.label: Forest claimed by both Britain and the United States

shots.on_screen_text: The disputed forest, between the two claims

paragraphs.text: People did settle the edge of it. In June 1785 a group of Acadian families, French speakers whose people had been expelled from Nova Scotia by the British a generation earlier, paddled up the St. John River and raised a wooden cross where they landed, near today's St. David. Five years later a count found a hundred and seventy-four people in the upper valley. Their descendants still live along that river, and many still speak French.

shots.on_screen_text: The St. John River at St. David

stat.label: Acadian families land on the upper St. John River
stat.source: acadian.org; University of Maine at Fort Kent

shots.on_screen_text: The St. John River below Madawaska
The Acadian landing cross, St. David

stat.label: People in the upper St. John Valley, 1790 count
stat.source: Census of Lower Canada, via acadian.org

shots.on_screen_text: Bienvenue: the welcome sign in Madawaska

paragraphs.text: By the 1830s, lumbermen from both sides were cutting the same trees. In February 1839 Maine sent an armed posse north from Bangor to throw out the New Brunswick loggers. The loggers seized Maine's land agent in the middle of the night. Maine called up its militia. Britain moved soldiers in. In Washington, Congress authorized fifty thousand men and ten million dollars in case of war. It is called the Aroostook War. Nobody was killed in battle. About thirty-eight men died of accidents and disease. In March, General Winfield Scott arrived and talked both sides down. That autumn the US Army began building Fort Kent, on the St. John, to hold the line.

shots.on_screen_text: Bangor, where the posse set out

stat.label: Authorized by Congress, with $10 million, in case of war over Maine, 1839
About 38 deaths in the Aroostook War, all from accident and disease

paragraphs.text: Three years later, in August 1842, Daniel Webster and Lord Ashburton split the difference. The United States got about seven thousand square miles, Britain about five thousand. The new line followed the St. John River for much of the way, which is why Maine's top edge looks the way it does. But a line on a map does not fill a forest. Even after 1842, almost nobody moved up there. The next reason is the simplest one: the weather.

shots.on_screen_text: The St. John River: Canada above, Maine below
The forest south of the St. John

paragraphs.text: Reason three. It is cold, and the summer is short. This forest has always been hard on people. In 1775, early in the Revolution, Benedict Arnold marched about eleven hundred men up the Kennebec to attack Quebec. He planned on a hundred and eighty miles. It turned out to be about three hundred and fifty. The men got lost in the swamps of the height of land, on today's Quebec border, and on the far side rapids smashed their boats and the food ran out. More than a third of the men turned back. About six hundred reached the St. Lawrence, half-starved.

shots.on_screen_text: The Dead River, on Arnold's route

chart.title: Arnold's march to Quebec, 1775
chart.source: Wikipedia, Benedict Arnold's expedition to Quebec

shots.on_screen_text: The height of land on the Quebec border

stat.label: Arnold's men who reached the St. Lawrence, November 1775

paragraphs.text: Up at Caribou, in Aroostook County, the average January day is under twelve degrees Fahrenheit. It once hit minus forty-one. About ten feet of snow falls in an average winter. In the winter of 2007 and 2008 it was more than sixteen feet. And the time between the last spring frost and the first autumn frost is about a hundred and thirty days. That is just over four months to grow anything.

stat.label: Average January day in Caribou, 1991-2020
stat.source: NOAA / National Weather Service, Caribou records

shots.photo: File:Pancake ice on the Allagash River, Maine.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Ice forming on the Allagash River

stat.label: Average time between the last spring frost and the first autumn frost at Caribou
stat.source: NOAA / National Weather Service, Caribou records

paragraphs.text: And most of the north was never farmland anyway. It is rolling hills, lakes and bogs, and what grows best is spruce and fir. Government climate scientists say Maine's growing season has been getting longer, but up north it is still short. By the Forest Service's count, about eighty-nine percent of Maine's land is forest. That is the highest share of any state.

shots.on_screen_text: Bogs and lakes in the North Woods
Spruce and fir near Moosehead Lake

document.text: The growing season in Maine has also lengthened.
document.source: NOAA NCICS, State Climate Summary: Maine

stat.label: Share of Maine's land that is forest, the most of any state
stat.source: USDA Forest Service, Forests of Maine 2021

paragraphs.text: There was one exception. In the far northeast, around Presque Isle, Caribou and Houlton, the land is gentler, and one crop loved the cool summers: potatoes. The first was planted near Houlton in 1807. When the railroad arrived late in the 1800s, Aroostook became a potato empire. Much of the early crop went to starch factories. Schools closed in autumn so children could help bring in the crop. Many high schools in Aroostook still close for up to two weeks every fall for the harvest. By 1947 Maine was growing potatoes on a hundred and eighty-six thousand acres, and it led the country in potatoes.

shots.photo: File:Farms in the Aroostook County, Me., Oct. 1940 - potatoes LCCN2017877406.jpg
File:Houlton, Me. Aroostook County seat. LOC 75693242.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Houlton, the county seat, in the 1890s
Presque Isle, on the Aroostook River

stat.label: Aroostook potatoes in 1890, much of the crop for starch

shots.photo: File:Children gathering potatoes on a large farm, vicinity of Caribou, Aroostook County, Me. Schools do not open until the potatoes are harvested LCCN2017877412.jpg

stat.label: Harvest break at most Aroostook high schools, 2024
Potatoes planted in Maine in 1947

paragraphs.text: Then the potato moved west. Idaho, with irrigation, bigger fields and better shipping, passed Maine in 1957. Maine still grows a lot of potatoes, almost all of them in Aroostook, but by 2021 the fields covered about fifty-eight thousand acres. Machines replaced the hands that picked them. So the north had long winters, short summers, and its one great crop found a better home. What kept people there was the work in the woods and the mills. And then that went too.

chart.title: Potato acres planted in Maine
chart.source: Maine Atlas; USDA via Bangor Daily News

shots.on_screen_text: A potato farm near Presque Isle

paragraphs.text: Reason four. The jobs left. For more than a century, logs from the north woods traveled by water. Every spring, crews drove them down the rivers on the snowmelt, all the way to the mills. A law passed in 1971 banned the drives after 1976, and by the mid-1970s the last ones had run down the Kennebec. The last big drive, in November 1975, brought television crews from around the country. Trucks took over, on private roads, and fewer men were needed in the woods.

stat.label: The last year river log drives were allowed in Maine (law of 1971)
stat.source: Maine law of 1971, via Central Maine and Down East

shots.photo: File:Sit Anywhere Woodsman relaxing after lunch during the spring pulpwood drive on the Brown Company timber holdings in Maine. May 1943. (40944955493).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Woodsmen on a spring pulpwood drive, Maine, 1943
The Golden Road at Ripogenus Dam

paragraphs.text: Then came a caterpillar. In the 1970s and 80s the spruce budworm ate its way through the spruce and fir of eastern Canada and northern Maine, across an estimated hundred and thirty-six million acres. Planes sprayed Maine's forest with insecticide, three and a half million acres in 1976 alone. Maine lost an estimated twenty to twenty-five million cords of wood, about a fifth of its spruce and fir. Whole stands of dead fir had to be cut in a hurry, and the companies kept cutting.

stat.label: Spruce budworm outbreak, eastern Canada and northern Maine, 1970s-80s

shots.on_screen_text: Spruce and fir forest, northern Maine in October

stat.label: Share of Maine's spruce and fir lost to the budworm outbreak

shots.on_screen_text: Spruce and fir today, northern Maine in winter

paragraphs.text: The paper mills were the biggest employers. In 1899 Great Northern began building a mill on the Penobscot River at Millinocket. When it opened the next year it was the world's largest paper mill, and a town grew around it in the forest. By 1970 Millinocket had seven thousand seven hundred people. Then newspapers shrank, owners changed, and the company went bankrupt in 2003. By 2014 the mills at Millinocket and East Millinocket had both closed. In 2020 Millinocket had about four thousand one hundred people.

shots.photo: File:Closely spaced mill-era homes in Millinocket, Maine.jpg

stat.label: People in Millinocket at the 1970 census
Great Northern Paper goes bankrupt

paragraphs.text: And then the Cold War ended. In 1953 the Air Force opened a base near Limestone, in the far northeast corner of Maine. It was described as the closest point in the continental United States to Europe, and for a bomber base that was the point. Its main runway was more than two miles long. Its bombers were B-36s at first, then B-52s. It also had the first site in the country built just to store and assemble atomic weapons. In 1988 about three thousand eight hundred airmen and a thousand civilians worked there.

shots.on_screen_text: Loring Air Force Base from above

shots.photo: File:Nose Hangar, Limestone Air Force Base, Limestone, Maine - DPLA - 83b68f60d44007fcd737e00c1b6e9cf6.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A bomber in a nose hangar at Limestone, 1950s
A storage bunker in Loring's weapons area

paragraphs.text: In 1991 a commission decided the Air Force had more bomber bases than it needed. Loring closed on the thirtieth of September 1994. Limestone had over thirteen thousand people in 1960. By 2000 it had two thousand three hundred. In 2020, about fifteen hundred. Aroostook County as a whole peaked at a hundred and six thousand people in 1960. In 2020 it had sixty-seven thousand.

shots.photo: File:Loring Air Force Base 1982 - Hangar - panoramio.jpg

stat.label: Loring Air Force Base closes

paragraphs.text: When it closed, the region lost thousands of military and civilian jobs. A state estimate had put nearly a fifth of the local economy on the base. Today part of the old base is an industrial park, and part of it is the Aroostook National Wildlife Refuge. The bunkers that once held the bombs are still there, in the grass.

stat.label: Share of the regional economy tied to Loring, state planning office estimate
stat.source: Maine State Planning Office, via press reports

shots.on_screen_text: The old base buildings, now an industrial park
Old weapons bunkers, Aroostook National Wildlife Refuge

paragraphs.text: So the work left. But some of the emptiness of northern Maine is no accident at all. Some of it was chosen.

Reason five. People decided to keep it wild. In 1846 Henry David Thoreau went up Katahdin, Maine's highest mountain. Today it is the northern end of the Appalachian Trail, more than two thousand miles from Georgia. Coming down, he wrote that up there he had felt the presence of a force not bound to be kind to man. Contact, he wrote. Who are we? Where are we? The mountain stayed with one man in particular.

document.text: There was clearly felt the presence of a force not bound to be kind to man.
document.source: Henry David Thoreau, The Maine Woods
document.highlight: not bound to be kind to man

shots.photo: File:Appalachian Trail and view of Mount Katahdin, Maine LCCN2011630252.tif

paragraphs.text: Percival Baxter, who became governor of Maine in 1921, wanted the state to make a park around Katahdin. That year the bill for it failed. So he did it himself. He bought about six thousand acres, Katahdin included, and in 1931 gave it to Maine on one condition: that it stay forever in its natural wild state. He kept buying and giving until 1962. More than two hundred thousand acres in all. Inside the park there is still no electricity, no running water and no paved road.

shots.on_screen_text: Katahdin and the land around it

stat.label: Percival Baxter gives Katahdin to Maine, on condition it stay wild

shots.on_screen_text: Baxter State Park, the northern half

stat.label: Percival Baxter's gifts to Maine, 1931 to 1962
stat.source: Baxter's letter to the Maine Legislature, 1963

paragraphs.text: In 1966 Maine voters protected the Allagash, ninety-two miles of lakes and river through the heart of the north woods. The bond to pay for it passed with sixty-eight percent of the vote. In 1970 it became the first state-run river in the national system of wild and scenic rivers. You can paddle it for a week and see no town.

stat.label: Maine voters for the Allagash Wilderness Waterway bond, November 1966

shots.on_screen_text: The Allagash River heading north in October

paragraphs.text: And in 2016 Roxanne Quimby, who made a fortune with Burt's Bees, gave about eighty-seven thousand five hundred acres east of Baxter to the federal government, and President Obama made it a national monument. A national park needs an act of Congress. A monument does not, so that is what she asked for. She added twenty million dollars for its upkeep and a pledge to raise twenty million more. Many people in the mill towns fought it. They feared it would close the woods to hunting, snowmobiles and logging. Between 1990 and 2015, about four million acres of the north woods were put under some kind of conservation.

shots.on_screen_text: Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument

stat.label: Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument, 24 August 2016

shots.photo: File:Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument on August 17, 2024 visit by the United States Department of the Interior - 19.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: The monument's land on the East Branch

stat.label: Quimby's endowment for the monument, and her pledge to raise as much again

shots.photo: File:Closely spaced mill-era homes in Millinocket, Maine.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Logging roads beside the monument in winter

paragraphs.text: So put it together. The land was sold in blocks before anyone could settle it, to owners who wanted trees, not towns. The border was fought over until 1842. The winters are long and the summers short, and the potato moved west. The log drives, the mills and the air base all closed. And the people of Maine chose to keep part of it wild, forever.

shots.on_screen_text: Private forest, northern Maine in winter

paragraphs.text: And the north is still shrinking. Between 2010 and 2020 Aroostook County lost about one in fifteen of its people. Maine as a whole now has the oldest population of any state.

stat.label: Median age in Maine, 2020: the highest of any state
stat.source: US Census Bureau, 2020 census, via CNN and Boston.com

paragraphs.text: Northern Maine is not empty because nobody wanted it. It is empty because, for two hundred years, the people who owned it wanted it to grow trees. Next time you look at a map of the eastern United States, look at the top right corner. That big blank is what is often called the largest block of undeveloped forest east of the Mississippi.

Here is my question for you. If someone gave you a cabin in the north woods, at the end of a private logging road, an hour of gravel from the nearest town, would you take it, or is that too far from everything?

ask.text: A cabin in the North Woods?

youtube.title: Why Almost Nobody Lives in Northern Maine
youtube.description: Almost half of Maine has no town government at all: more than 14,000 square miles where about 8,300 people lived at the 2020 census. This video goes through the five reasons the north stayed empty: the wild lands Massachusetts sold to timber and paper companies, a border with Britain nobody could draw until 1842, the long winters and the potato's move west, the end of the log drives, the paper mills and Loring Air Force Base, and the people who chose to keep Katahdin and the Allagash wild.
